notes.meaning: Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, put Zedekiah on Judah's throne and gave him that name. His old name was Mattaniah. He replaced Coniah, also called Jehoiachin or Jeconiah. Some older writers think the short name "Coniah" was used to show disrespect.

The king, his officials and the ordinary people all ignored what God said through Jeremiah. They had just watched Coniah be punished and carried off, yet they did not learn from it. Calvin points out that God did not need to speak from heaven. Speaking through His prophet was enough to leave them without excuse.

Zedekiah was afraid of the Babylonians, so he sent men to ask Jeremiah to pray for the nation. Matthew Henry sees some good in this, because it is right to ask others to pray for us when we are in trouble. But Zedekiah wanted the prophet's prayers while refusing his advice. Calvin adds that true believers ask others to pray and also pray to God themselves.
At this point Jeremiah was a free man. He could move around the city and speak with people. The verse prepares us for the prison time that comes later in the chapter.

An Egyptian army, probably sent by Pharaoh Hophra, marched out to help Judah. So the Babylonian army (the "Chaldeans") left Jerusalem to face them. To the people it looked like rescue had come. Matthew Henry notes that a pause in trouble often makes people feel falsely safe.
God's answer was plain. Egypt's army would go home without saving anyone. Matthew Henry sums up the lesson: if God does not help us, no one else can.
The Babylonians would come back, capture Jerusalem and burn it. Matthew Henry says God directs even armies that do not know Him, and they end up carrying out His purposes.

God warns the people not to fool themselves by thinking the enemy has gone for good. Matthew Henry observes that we are often deceived because we deceive ourselves, and God's word is given to open our eyes.

Even if only wounded Babylonian soldiers were left lying in their tents, they would still get up and burn the city. The picture shows that Jerusalem's fall was certain. It would come by God's judgment, not by Babylon's strength. When God has decided to do something, the tools He uses may look weak, but they will still do the work.

While the Babylonians were away, Jeremiah set out for the land of Benjamin, probably to his hometown of Anathoth. The phrase about his "portion" is unclear. Some take it to mean he went to collect his share of family land or its harvest, perhaps the field he had bought in chapter 32. Others think he simply wanted to get away from a city where his preaching was doing no good.

At the city gate that faced Benjamin, a guard captain named Irijah arrested him. Irijah accused him of going over to the enemy. Jeremiah had long said Babylon would win, so his enemies used that against him. Some suggest Irijah was the grandson of the false prophet Hananiah and held a grudge.

Jeremiah firmly denied the charge, but Irijah would not listen and took him to the officials. Matthew Henry says that when we are falsely accused, we may deny it and leave our case with God, who judges fairly. Calvin notes that God's servants often face lies about them, even when they are innocent.

The angry officials had Jeremiah beaten and locked up. There was no proof and no fair hearing. A scribe named Jonathan had his house turned into a prison. Calvin observes that people ruled by anger cannot judge fairly.

This prison was an underground pit with small cells cut into its sides. It was dark, damp and cramped. Jeremiah was left there for a long time. Matthew Henry contrasts the comfort of the guilty officials with the suffering of God's faithful servant.

Later the king brought Jeremiah to his palace in secret. He was afraid or ashamed for his officials to see him asking the prophet. He hoped for a better word from God, but Jeremiah told him plainly that he would be handed over to Babylon's king. That took great courage, since Jeremiah's life was in the king's hands. God's message was the same in private as it was in public.

Jeremiah asked what crime he had committed to deserve prison. Speaking God's hard message was not a wrong against the king or the people. Calvin compares this to Daniel, who said he had done the king no wrong by obeying God.
The prophets who promised that Babylon would never come had been proven wrong. Babylon had already come, just as Jeremiah said. This showed that Jeremiah was innocent and truly sent by God.

Jeremiah humbly begged not to be sent back to that pit, because he feared he would die there. He was human and dreaded death, yet he never let fear stop him from doing his duty. Matthew Henry puts it this way: Jeremiah was bold as a lion for God's cause but gentle as a lamb in his own. He made no complaint against the officials who had wronged him.

The king moved Jeremiah to the courtyard of the guard, a far better place. He also ordered that Jeremiah be given a loaf of bread each day until the city's bread ran out. Zedekiah still did not set him free. The older writers see God's care here: He moved the king's heart and fed His servant during the famine, as Psalm 37:19 promises.
